extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, federal trial judges, and law students studying patent infringement procedure and damages
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative standards for conducting and reviewing patent infringement trials (jury, judge, or referee), taxation of costs, preparation of bills of exceptions, appellate scope via writ of error, and measures of damages (royalty, lost monopoly, reasonable royalty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive nature of judge's findings on facts
rubrics_metrics.description: If the judge makes findings of fact (including special findings), those findings are conclusive on the facts found; on appeal the Circuit Court of Appeals may examine only the sufficiency of the facts found to support the judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the judge misunderstood or misapplied tests (e.g., novelty or infringement), the finding of fact remains conclusive on appeal from a judgment at law because appellate review is limited to the sufficiency of the facts found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on review when judge simply finds for defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: When the judge simply finds for the defendant and enters judgment accordingly, review in the Circuit Court of Appeals is available only by the regular common-law method (bill of exceptions and writ of error) and only on pure questions of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual issues are not carried on a writ of error in such cases; the appellate review is confined to legal questions properly preserved and presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of judicial factual finding to support judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: When a judge finds facts such as lack of novelty or noninfringement and enters judgment for defendant, the fact so found is sufficient to support the judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appellate court will not retry facts; it will consider only whether the facts found are sufficient to sustain the legal judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special findings must relate to fundamental facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where special findings of fact are used to enable appellate review, those findings should relate to the fundamental facts of the case, not merely to conclusions of fact deducible from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special findings framed as conclusions rather than as foundational facts can frustrate effective appellate review; parties should aim to have referees/judges find underlying operative facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to institute trial by referee
rubrics_metrics.description: A trial by referee may be instituted by a clerk entry at parties' request or by a written stipulation signed and filed; the court may issue an order referring the case to the named referee and directing him to hear and determine issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once referred, the referee must hear parties, decide controversies, and make a report to the court. Parties may except in writing to the report; court may adopt, reject, or recommit the report with directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of referee's report (special vs general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A referee's report may be special (setting forth details of the evidence) or general (giving only the conclusions to which the evidence carried the mind of the referee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special reports detail evidentiary bases and better support appellate review; courts may remand for further direction if report is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: State law governs referee trials absent federal statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Because trial by referee is not provided for by any United States statute, its details are regulated by the laws of the particular State in which the trial is had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must consult relevant state statutes and rules for methods of taking testimony before referees, timing of reports, weight attached to reports, and practice to secure judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry of judgments following verdicts/findings/reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments follow verdicts of juries, findings of judges, or reports of referees; unless set aside, reconsidered, or rejected/recommitted, the clerk enters judgment under authority of the judge and that entry is binding as the act of the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District Courts do not routinely require a rule to enter judgment; the clerk acts under judicial authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court power to increase judgment (relation to damages chapter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances which justify courts in entering judgments for any sum above the amount of the verdict, finding, or report, but not exceeding three times the amount thereof, are discussed in the damages chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the court has similar power where damages are ascertained by judge or referee has not been judicially decided, but is generally doubted to differ; practitioners should consult damages doctrine on increased damages and treble awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff entitlement to costs in patent infringement judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: All plaintiffs who secure judgments for infringements of patents may recover costs, even for nominal damages, subject to specified exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs are presumptively recoverable for successful plaintiffs; exceptions (see next criterion) must be shown by defendant to avoid cost award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to plaintiff's recovery of costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff cannot recover costs where it appears at trial that one or more patent claims are void for lack of being the subject of a patent, for want of invention, or for want of novelty, and no proper disclaimer was filed before suit; where only a small part of alleged infringement is found; where defendant offered before suit to submit to patent and pay a definite sum as damages equal to plaintiff’s recovery; and where parts of the patents or claims sued upon are not recovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In partial-success situations, whether plaintiff recovers costs on successful patents/claims is case-specific and may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxable items of costs limited to statute and court rules
rubrics_metrics.description: All items of costs taxable in a United States court are specified in the United States statutes or in rules of that court authorized by statute; taxing officers must compare suggested items to those enumerated and tax only those.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No expenses other than taxable costs may lawfully be inserted in a cost bill; where statutes are clear no further explanation is needed, but some items have required judicial construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: One attorney's docket fee taxable per case
rubrics_metrics.description: One attorney's docket fee is taxable in each case against the defeated party; there is no warrant for taxing the unsuccessful party with a separate docket fee for each of the adversary’s attorneys or for each term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney deposition fees cannot be taxed in favor of an attorney as extra compensation; taxable attorney's fees are taxed in favor of clients to help them pay their attorneys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerk fees generally taxable but copies for own use are not
rubrics_metrics.description: Clerk of court fees are generally taxable against the defeated party, but items like copies of the record ordered by a party for his own use are not taxable against the opponent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extent to which clerks may make records and charge defeated parties depends on each court's rules; in equity actions, Section 750 of the Revised Statutes regulates such matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner/magistrate deposition fee limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees of a commissioner or magistrate taking a deposition are strictly limited to twenty cents for each hundred words in the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These fees are generally taxable against the defeated party, but not if the deposition is not offered in evidence; by analogy, magistrates' fees are not taxable on depositions offered but not admitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness fees taxable rules and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Witness fees are generally taxable against the defeated party whether testimony was oral or by deposition, but are not taxable when deposition is not offered or, if offered, not admitted; fees for more than three witnesses to one fact are not taxable unless necessity shown by affidavit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a defeated party is taxable with fees for witnesses who testified without a subpoena is unsettled; service by a private person suffices. Parties should support claims for additional witness fees with affidavit showing necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxability of witness fees in special circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Witness fees are taxable in favor of a defendant though his witnesses are not examined because the action is not prosecuted; where witnesses attend more than once due to a stipulated postponement, fees are taxed as continuous attendance; witnesses from a distance detained over Sunday are entitled to Sunday fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules emphasize fairness in compensating witness attendance tied to the litigation's practical circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and review of taxation of costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxation of costs may be made at the time the judgment is entered (preferred), but a blank for costs may be left in judgment and later filled nunc pro tunc after affirmation by the Circuit Court of Appeals; legality of taxation may be reviewed by the Circuit Court of Appeals if the case is taken there to secure reversal as to damages as well as costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where only nominal damages and costs are adjudged, defendant cannot take the case to the Circuit Court of Appeals solely to reverse or reduce costs; timing and procedure for retaxation/appeal must be observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerk as primary taxing officer under judge's direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Clerks of District Courts are the primary taxing officers, but they perform duties under the general or particular direction of the judges, who may properly give directions when entering judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge can direct how taxation is to be handled at the time of entering judgment; parties should be attentive to judicial instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for retaxation and appeal of costs
rubrics_metrics.description: If dissatisfied with taxation, defeated party may move for retaxation; such a motion should show colorable ground for error, give opposite party notice, and pay costs occasioned; to appeal a retaxation result, the appellant must secure an itemized bill and show items are unwarranted by statute or relate to immaterial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These proceedings generally must occur in the term judgment is entered unless a blank was left for costs pending writ of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writ of error scope in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A writ of error from any Circuit Court of Appeals will carry any action at law for patent infringement from any subordinate court, regardless of damages amount and irrespective of trial type, but it cannot carry questions of fact — it secures review of questions of law or, where special findings were made, whether facts found suffice to support judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate practitioners should frame issues as legal or demonstrate proper special factual findings to bring factual sufficiency before the appellate tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and form of bills of exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills of exceptions, allowed and signed or sealed by the judge, are the only mode to prepare trial questions of law for transmission to an appellate court via writ of error; incorporated papers with the substantial characteristics of a bill will be treated as such even if not so titled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bills should contain no more than necessary to present the reviewable questions; irrelevant or excessive material wastes appellate resources and may hinder review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content requirements for bills concerning pleadings and witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill of exceptions should state only what is necessary: where questions relate only to pleadings, insert pleadings only; where they relate to competency of a witness, show that the witness was offered and accepted/rejected and that due notice (as to novelty) was served; where particular answers were excluded, the bill must contain those answers and show materiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When particular questions were excluded and not answered, the bill must show facts the party offered to prove and their materiality; when a question was admitted and answered, the bill must show the answer to enable appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bills for charges/instructions to jury — required content
rubrics_metrics.description: If the review concerns instructions, the bill should set forth the issues of the pleadings, the substance of the charge or refusal to charge, and whatever part of the evidence is necessary for the appellate court to decide the propriety of the lower court's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the substance (not necessarily verbatim) of charges to avoid wasting appellate time on incidental expressions; but if only charged matter is excepted to, the whole substance should be stated, otherwise omitted parts might have cured alleged faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of refused instructions in bills of exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a refusal to charge is excepted to, the bill must contain not only the refused instruction but also the whole substance of the charge actually given, so the appellate court can tell whether the refused instruction was substantially covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges are not bound to give requested instructions in the precise form requested if the substance of relevant law is adequately embodied in the charge given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence inclusion rules for bills attacking charges
rubrics_metrics.description: If only charged matter is excepted to, the bill should not include evidence. But if a refusal to charge is excepted to, the bill must contain the evidence to which the refused instruction relates or a statement of pertinent facts and that evidence was introduced tending to prove them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No court is bound to give an instruction that does not relate to the evidence; therefore a bill attacking a refusal must show the evidentiary basis for the requested instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of specific exceptions to instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific exceptions must be made to instructions to entitle the objector to appellate review of those instructions; if a requested instruction was unsound in any particular, refusal will be sustained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel should separate propositions of law carefully when framing requests for instructions so that one erroneous proposition does not nullify other sound ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for making exceptions to charges and bills of exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to charges or refusals must be made and noted while the jury is at the bar; bills of exceptions may be drawn up and signed by the judge any time before the expiration of the term unless the judge requires an earlier time and may, if not too late, be prepared after writ of error has been sued out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict adherence to timing rules is necessary to preserve issues for appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic measure of patent damages: plaintiff’s pecuniary injury
rubrics_metrics.description: The generic measure of damages is the pecuniary injury the plaintiff suffered by reason of the defendant's infringement — often the plaintiff's loss or failure to acquire a just and deserved gain; the magnitude must be ascertained to fix damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defendant's profits are not directly relevant in an action at law as a measure of plaintiff's damages (profits are not recoverable in law and may not reflect plaintiff's loss).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadmissibility of defendant's profits as direct measure in actions at law
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of profits derived by the defendant has no direct relevancy to plaintiff's damages in an action at law: (1) defendant's profits are not recoverable in law; (2) they may be much larger or smaller than plaintiff's pecuniary injury and thus are not a reliable measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patentee elected (in equity) to recover infringer's profits, he cannot thereafter recover those same damages in an action at law for the same infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative method for ascertaining plaintiff's damages
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain the plaintiff's pecuniary injury, determine the difference between his pecuniary condition after the infringement and what his condition would have been if the infringement had not occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depending on patentee practices (licensed vs kept monopoly), the difference may be measured as royalties the patentee would have received or monopoly profits the patentee would have realized absent the infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three primary methods of assessing patent damages
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several methods: (1) using the plaintiff's established royalty as the measure of damages (primary); (2) ascertaining what defendant's interference with plaintiff's close monopoly prevented the plaintiff from deriving (lost monopoly profits) (secondary); (3) proving what would have been a reasonable royalty (tertiary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these methods separately; choice depends on evidence available, plaintiff’s licensing history, market structure, and proof of lost sales or royalties. Each method is subject to tests and objections from the opposing party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections and tests applicable to royalties as damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalties invoked by plaintiffs or defendants are subject to different classes of tests: defendants may apply certain tests to challenge a plaintiff-invoked royalty; plaintiffs may apply other tests when a defendant invokes a royalty to limit recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text flags that royalties as measures of damages are often litigated with competing evidentiary tests; practitioners should prepare to justify royalty methodology or to rebut a royalty-based limitation.
